title: Co-Creation Done Right
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli argues that co-creation is a disciplined design method, not a buzzword, and that most organisational workshops fail because they become performative rituals of sticky notes and vague themes. She distinguishes co-creation from interviews and focus groups: participants build and shape solutions as collaborators rather than being studied. She says it suits generative stages of complex problems, illustrated by her work on the UK Data Service 2024-2030 strategy, and backfires where people cannot speak freely, such as a junior employee with a senior manager present. The piece lists workable formats such as affinity clustering, journey mapping and dot voting, and ties them to the Double Diamond. She closes with design principles (activities over themes, groups of three to five, protected synthesis time, thorough capture) and common pitfalls such as overstuffed agendas and ignored power dynamics.
points: Co-creation turns participants into co-designers and yields experiential data that interviews cannot, but only for generative, complex problems.
Psychological safety and power dynamics decide whether co-creation works; personal or charged topics call for one-to-one interviews or anonymous surveys.
Good sessions use two or three building methods with ample sense-making time rather than packing the agenda.
Small groups with assigned roles, protected synthesis and full documentation turn a workshop into usable output.
The goal is clarity and shared ownership rather than consensus, which separates buy-in from lip service.
quotes: Every organisation claims to value collaboration. Yet, in practice, too many co-creation sessions (e.g. workshops) end up as performative rituals: sticky notes, vague themes and little follow-through.

Unlike interviews, which aim to extract stories, or focus groups, which explore shared experiences, co-creation brings people into the process as collaborators. Participants help shape the solution, not just comment on it.

That said, co-creation isn’t always the answer. It can backfire when participants can’t speak freely or feel unsafe sharing candid thoughts. Imagine a very junior employee asked to contribute ideas in a room with their senior manager… it’s unlikely you’ll get candour!
You don’t need to run all of these in a single session. In fact, the best co-creation workshops use just two or three methods, with plenty of time for sense-making in between.
Don’t skip the synthesis. The magic is in how your participants make sense of the shared challenge together. Build in time for small groups to report back and reflect.
Treating co-creation as consensus: Agreement isn’t the goal. Clarity is. ¬I Tension is part of the process, and you should capture this accurately.
What comes out of a well-designed co-creation process is shared ownership of what happens next. That’s the difference between buy-in and resistance, between lip service and lasting change.
